After 58 years of history, the Silver City Café (銀都冰室) recently posted a "glorious closure" notice at its premises. The shop has been gradually clearing out and emptying in recent days, with its招牌 and marble slabs at the entrance already removed.

After 58 years of history, the Silver City Café recently posted a "glorious closure" notice at its premises, stating that it had walked through 58 years of storms together, expressing gratitude for years of support, and offering sincere apologies for not being able to say goodbye earlier, as well as deep reluctance to part. The shop has been gradually clearing out and emptying in recent days, with its招牌 and marble slabs at the entrance already removed. Over the past few days, many regular customers and neighbourhood residents have passed by the shop, exchanging farewells and taking souvenir photos with the owner and staff.

Many regular customers and neighbourhood residents have passed by the shop, exchanging farewells and chatting with the owner and staff.

Elderly original resident: They are friends, not customers

80-year-old Grandma Fung (馮婆婆) greeted the owner enthusiastically and chatted warmly the moment she saw him. Grandma Fung moved in when Wah Fu Estate (華富邨) was first built and has lived there for nearly 60 years. Watching Silver City Café pass from its first-generation owners, the Yuen couple, to the second-generation daughter who now manages it, and now seeing it close gloriously, she said, "Of course I'm reluctant to see it go. Every time I come down I'm so happy — ha ha ha — watching them for decades, watching them grow up, study, and get married."

Helping staff tidy up when they are busy

She used to visit occasionally, but since retiring a few years ago she has come almost every morning to "have a meal," growing close to the staff and the owner. Each morning she would read newspapers and magazines, fiddle with her phone, chat a while, laugh for a bit, then leave. "We've become like good friends — when you go in everyone's laughing and joking. They're friends, not customers." Sometimes, when she saw the staff were busy, she would voluntarily help clear the bowls and plates and wipe the tables after eating: "So when customers come there'll be tables for them." When staff were having their meals, she didn't mind sitting with them; knowing she wasn't a picky eater, they would generously share their staff meals and leftover dishes with her.

"Life is about gathering and parting"

Faced with parting, Grandma Fung said what she would miss most is this friendship, but she also understands that the owner deserves a rest, and redevelopment is a wheel that cannot be stopped. "I tell myself not to be too sad — life is about gathering and parting. We've been lucky to have gathered for so many years."

Grandma Fung's unit faces the sea, and she says frankly that she likes this home. "If it weren't good, I wouldn't have lived here so long — I moved in and I'll stay until they tear it down." She adds, however, that she is quite philosophical about it: "What's the point of kicking up a fuss? That's government policy — are the buildings all that structurally sound?" Her unit is expected to relocate only after 2030, and she laughs that at her age, "We'll worry about it then… (the new estate) will be built no matter what, but whether I'll still be around to see it is another matter."

26-year-old Ah-ching (阿程) has lived in Wah Fu Estate since birth, and says he really enjoys cha chaan teng and ice rooms (冰室). Ah-ching says the cha chaan teng has many of his "comfort foods." (Photo provided by interviewee Ah-ching)

Young man who grew up in Wah Fu Estate: Lost a habit

26-year-old Ah-ching has lived in Wah Fu Estate since birth, and says he really enjoys cha chaan teng and ice rooms, frequently visiting the Wah Fu Café (華富冰室) and Silver City Café within the estate. Upon learning of Silver City's closure in the early hours of 1 August, he felt upset and could not sleep that night, saying frankly that he had lost a place that made him feel at ease. The place is full of Ah-ching's memories — for example, more than ten years ago he would often eat there with a bus driver friend, who has since passed away. Last year he also took a Japanese friend to the shop; the friend was amazed that such an old establishment served customers of all ages, and gave high praise to the red bean ice, but sadly never got to return — Silver City has now closed.

(Photo provided by interviewee Ah-ching)

Ah-ching says the cha chaan teng holds many of his "comfort foods," such as toast and milk tea, while in the ice room — from choosing a seat upon entering, to the waiter bringing tea, to him ordering his meal — every step is a place that makes him feel safe and secure when he is emotionally unsettled. "They have a way of making you feel taken care of." He especially liked sitting by the window at Silver City Café, without being hurried, looking out at the podium of the Wah Fu Shopping Centre across the way and the blue sky: "Just looking at this scene is already a kind of happiness."

Losing Silver City Café, Ah-ching says, is losing a habit and a last refuge. "As these traditional ice rooms disappear one by one, where can I still go?… I really don't know where I can go." With the redevelopment of Wah Fu, the gradual departure of old shops is a foreseeable thing, and Ah-ching describes it as a helpless kind of acceptance: "Does my reluctance really mean they won't demolish it? No." But he believes people are free, and since he doesn't want to forget, "you have your own way — you can choose to remember."

Only about one-third of Wah On Building shops still operating

As for the first phase of redevelopment, which is divided into two parts, residents of Wah On Building (華安樓) and Wah Lok Building (華樂樓) in Phase 1a are selecting flats this month, and are expected to begin moving into units on Wah King Street between October and November, with all required to relocate by the end of July next year. Phase 1b — Wah Cheong, Wah Tai and Wah Kin Buildings — together with the receiving estates Wah Lok Path and Wah Fu North Estate, are expected to be occupied in 2028 and 2030 respectively, with the target of clearing all residents by March 2031.

As the first batch of affected buildings, most of the ground-floor shops in Wah On Building have already shuttered, with only about one-third still in operation — including "Lai Wah Salon" (麗華髮廊), "Wah Cheong Store" (華昌士多), "Golden Crown Snacks" (金冠零食), "Pak Tat Laundry" (百達洗衣) and "Kam Kee Cart Noodles" (鑑記車仔麵) — all long-established neighbourhood shops expected to continue operating until they must relocate.

As for whether they will move to the new receiving estate to continue business, some shops say they are still considering. A staff member at Golden Crown Snacks said that if the Housing Department can arrange a shop, they would hopefully continue to operate; however, the septuagenarian Mr Chan, owner of Wah Cheong Store, worries that having to move into a shopping centre in future would mean high rent and fewer customers, making business difficult. He expects his store — with over 40 years of history — to come to an end when Wah On Building is demolished: "Retirement — I'm done."
